claim: RbmA is composed of tandem fibronectin type III (FnIII) domains
source: We previously determined the crystal structure of RbmA, which showed that RbmA is composed of tandem fibronectin type III (FnIII) domains (Giglio et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Giglio et al., 2013) that determined the crystal structure

claim: RbmA binds VPS directly
source: Here, we show that RbmA binds VPS directly to control the VPS-dependent formation of higher-order structures that modulate biofilm architecture and that V. cholerae biofilms can be fine-tuned by RbmA structural dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including NMR spectroscopy experiments showing VPS binding

claim: RbmA uses a binary structural switch within its first fibronectin type III (FnIII-1) domain to control RbmA structural dynamics
source: We demonstrate that RbmA binds VPS directly and uses a binary structural switch within its first fibronectin type III (FnIII-1) domain to control RbmA structural dynamics and the formation of VPS-dependent higher-order structures.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data including NMR spectroscopy and SEC-MALS analysis showing two discrete structural states

claim: The structural switch in FnIII-1 regulates interactions in trans with the FnIII-2 domain, leading to open (monomeric) or closed (dimeric) interfaces
source: The structural switch in FnIII-1 regulates interactions in trans with the FnIII-2 domain, leading to open (monomeric) or closed (dimeric) interfaces.
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC-MALS data showing dimerization states and NMR data showing conformational changes

claim: The ability of RbmA to switch between open and closed states is important for V. cholerae biofilm formation
source: The ability of RbmA to switch between open and closed states is important for V. cholerae biofilm formation, as RbmA variants with switches that are locked in either of the two states lead to biofilms with altered architecture and structural integrity.
evidence: The claim is supported by biofilm formation assays comparing wild-type and mutant strains

claim: RbmA variants with switches locked in either of the two states lead to biofilms with altered architecture and structural integrity
source: The ability of RbmA to switch between open and closed states is important for V. cholerae biofilm formation, as RbmA variants with switches that are locked in either of the two states lead to biofilms with altered architecture and structural integrity.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantitative analysis of biofilm architecture in mutant strains

claim: Biofilm formation is critical for both aquatic and intestinal phases in the lifecycle of Vibrio cholerae
source: Biofilm formation is critical for both aquatic and intestinal phases in the lifecycle of the facultative human pathogen Vibrio cholerae, the causative agent of the severe diarrheal disease cholera (Teschler et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Teschler et al., 2015)

claim: The ability to form biofilms enhances growth and survival of V. cholerae outside the body of its mammalian host
source: The ability to form biofilms enhances growth and survival of the pathogen outside the body of its mammalian host by providing protection from a number of environmental stresses, including nutrient limitation and predation by protozoa and bacteriophages (Yildiz and Schoolnik, 1999; Matz et al., 2005; Beyhan and Yildiz, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Yildiz and Schoolnik, 1999; Matz et al., 2005; Beyhan and Yildiz, 2007)

claim: Growth in biofilms enhances transmission and induces a hyper-infectious phenotype in V. cholerae
source: Additionally, growth in biofilms enhances transmission and induces a hyper-infectious phenotype (Faruque et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Faruque et al., 2006)

claim: Production of biofilms by V. cholerae requires extracellular matrix components including VPS and the matrix proteins RbmA, RbmC, and Bap1
source: Production of biofilms by V. cholerae requires extracellular matrix components, such as the Vibrio exopolysaccharide (VPS) and the matrix proteins RbmA, RbmC, and Bap1 (Yildiz and Schoolnik, 1999; Fong et al., 2006; Fong and Yildiz, 2007; Fong et al., 2010; Absalon et al., 2011; Berk et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Yildiz and Schoolnik, 1999; Fong et al., 2006; Fong and Yildiz, 2007; Fong et al., 2010; Absalon et al., 2011; Berk et al., 2012)

claim: RbmA is thought to capture progeny to the founder cell, thereby enabling cell-cell adhesion and formation of cell clusters
source: RbmA is thought to capture progeny to the founder cell, thereby enabling cell-cell adhesion and formation of cell clusters (Berk et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Berk et al., 2012)

claim: RbmA controls the arrangements of V. cholerae cells relative to the substratum during biofilm development
source: Additionally, RbmA controls the arrangements of V. cholerae cells relative to the substratum during biofilm development, and in turn, governs development of mature biofilm architecture (Drescher et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Drescher et al., 2016)

claim: RbmA dimer is characterized by two distinct structures at the dimer interface in multiple crystal forms
source: The native RbmA dimer is characterized by two distinct structures at the dimer interface in multiple crystal forms, where residues 91 to 108 of FnIII-1 adopt so-called disordered-loop (D-loop, Figure 1A, top) or ordered-loop (O-loop, Figure 1A, bottom) conformations (Giglio et al., 2013; Maestre-Reyna et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous crystal structures (Giglio et al., 2013; Maestre-Reyna et al., 2013) and Figure 1A showing the two conformations

claim: In the O-loop conformation, the βc strand of the FnIII-1 domain is largely unfolded to facilitate a network of interactions between residue D97 and the FnIII-1 and FnIII-2 domains to stabilize the closed dimer interface
source: In the O-loop conformation, the βc strand of the FnIII-1 domain is largely unfolded to facilitate a network of interactions between residue D97 and the FnIII-1 and FnIII-2 domains to stabilize the closed dimer interface, whereas these interactions are abolished in the D-loop conformation (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: One key residue interacting with D97 in the O-loop conformation is FnIII-2 residue R234
source: One key residue interacting with D97 in the O-loop conformation is FnIII-2 residue R234.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in the figures

claim: The R234A mutant disrupted biofilm formation
source: We previously showed that the R234A mutant disrupted biofilm formation (Giglio et al., 2013), suggesting that regulation of this dimer interface might be important for RbmA function.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Giglio et al., 2013)

claim: The overlaid NMR spectra revealed several residues in the FnIII-2 domain exhibiting collinear chemical shifts reporting on a two-state equilibrium in fast exchange
source: The overlaid spectra revealed several residues in the FnIII-2 domain, which were distal from any mutation sites that exhibited collinear chemical shifts reporting on a two-state equilibrium in fast exchange, with populations of the two states tuned by different mutations (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The endpoints of the two-state equilibrium are punctuated by the R234A and D97A or D97K mutants
source: The endpoints of this two-state equilibrium are punctuated by the R234A and D97A or D97K mutants, suggesting that they represent discrete structural states of the switch.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data showing chemical shift patterns

claim: Each peak for the WT protein was located approximately halfway between the two endpoints, consistent with observations that the protein natively populates both states
source: Each peak for the WT protein was located approximately halfway between the two endpoints, consistent with observations that the protein natively populates both states (Giglio et al., 2013; Maestre-Reyna et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data and citations to previous crystal structures (Giglio et al., 2013; Maestre-Reyna et al., 2013)

claim: Mutations at D97 lock RbmA into the open, D-loop conformation
source: Comparing the 15N-1H TROSY-HSQC spectrum of 15N RbmA* to the full-length variants, we observed a striking similarity of the chemical shifts for the full-length D97 mutants and those of RbmA*, indicating that mutations at D97 lock RbmA into the open, D-loop conformation (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data comparing D97 mutants to RbmA* shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The R234A mutation locks RbmA into the more closed O-loop conformation
source: Based on the two states consistently observed in RbmA crystal structures (Giglio et al., 2013; Maestre-Reyna et al., 2013), this implies that the R234A mutation locks RbmA into the more closed O-loop conformation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from NMR data and previous crystal structures (Giglio et al., 2013; Maestre-Reyna et al., 2013)

claim: Both D97A and D97K mutants were predominantly monomeric
source: Consistent with a model where mutations at D97 eliminate O-loop interactions that stabilize the FnIII-1:FnIII-2 dimer interface, both D97A and D97K mutants were predominantly monomeric, while WT and R234A formed stable dimers under these conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 1D and Table 1

claim: WT and R234A RbmA formed stable dimers
source: Consistent with a model where mutations at D97 eliminate O-loop interactions that stabilize the FnIII-1:FnIII-2 dimer interface, both D97A and D97K mutants were predominantly monomeric, while WT and R234A formed stable dimers under these conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 1D and Table 1

claim: RbmA* was found predominantly in its expected monomeric state due to the absence of an intact FnIII-1 domain
source: RbmA* was also found predominantly in its expected monomeric state due to the absence of an intact FnIII-1 domain, although a small fraction (<10%) exhibited higher-order aggregation, likely due to retention of the unfolded FnIII-1 fragment (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The O-loop is required to stabilize the FnIII-1:FnIII-2 dimer interface
source: These data demonstrate that the O-loop is required to stabilize the FnIII-1:FnIII-2 dimer interface, and that formation of only one O-loop interface in the WT protein is sufficient to stabilize the RbmA dimer.
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC-MALS data showing dimerization states of mutants

claim: Formation of only one O-loop interface in the WT protein is sufficient to stabilize the RbmA dimer
source: These data demonstrate that the O-loop is required to stabilize the FnIII-1:FnIII-2 dimer interface, and that formation of only one O-loop interface in the WT protein is sufficient to stabilize the RbmA dimer.
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC-MALS data showing WT forms stable dimers

claim: The monomeric D97A mutant was rapidly proteolyzed down to a stable 13 kDa fragment comprising the FnIII-2 domain
source: The monomeric D97A mutant was rapidly proteolyzed down to a stable 13 kDa fragment comprising the FnIII-2 domain that was also observed to a lesser degree in the WT protein, but not in the R234A mutant (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by limited proteolysis data shown in Figure 2A–C

claim: The dimeric WT and R234A proteins both remained relatively stable to proteolysis and shared a higher molecular weight tryptic fragment
source: The dimeric WT and R234A proteins both remained relatively stable to proteolysis and shared a higher molecular weight tryptic fragment.
evidence: The claim is supported by limited proteolysis data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The relative protease-resistance of the R234A mutant in vitro is further evidence that it adopts a closed conformation relative to the D97A/D97K mutants
source: The relative protease-resistance of the R234A mutant in vitro is further evidence in that it adopts a closed conformation relative to the D97A/D97K mutants.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from limited proteolysis data

claim: RbmA undergoes a proteolytic cleavage in vivo
source: RbmA undergoes a proteolytic cleavage in vivo (Berk et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Berk et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2015)

claim: RbmA was readily cleaved in vivo in both planktonic and biofilm cultures
source: We found that RbmA was readily cleaved in vivo in both planktonic and biofilm cultures (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D and E

claim: D97A, D97K and R234A variants produced the expected proteolytic products in vivo
source: To determine how changes to this binary switch in the FnIII-1 domain might influence RbmA proteolytic cleavage, we analyzed in vivo proteolysis of RbmA in the D97A, D97K and R234A variants and found that they produced the expected proteolytic products (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F

claim: RbmA proteolysis is markedly decreased in a strain lacking all three proteases (HapA, PrtV and IvaP) reported to cleave RbmA
source: As a control, we included a strain lacking all three proteases (HapA, PrtV and IvaP) reported to cleave RbmA and showed that RbmA proteolysis is markedly decreased in this strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F

claim: In a strain lacking VPS, RbmA is completely degraded
source: In a strain lacking VPS, RbmA is completely degraded.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data

claim: RbmA proteolysis is decreased in the rugose variant, which is characterized by increased VPS production relative to the wild-type smooth strain
source: As expected, RbmA proteolysis is decreased in the rugose variant (Figure 2D), which is characterized by increased VPS production relative to the wild-type smooth strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: RbmA natively samples both the O-loop and D-loop states to regulate dimer interfaces and protease accessibility in vivo
source: Collectively, these data support a model in which RbmA natively samples both the O-loop and D-loop states to regulate dimer interfaces and protease accessibility in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including NMR, SEC-MALS, and proteolysis data

claim: Strains harboring the D97A and D97K mutations retained the colony corrugation pattern of the rugose parental strain
source: Strains harboring the D97A and D97K mutations retained the colony corrugation pattern of the rugose parental strain, while strains lacking RbmA (∆rbmA) or harboring the R234A mutation exhibited a marked decrease in colony corrugation (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony biofilm images shown in Figure 3A

claim: Strains lacking RbmA (∆rbmA) or harboring the R234A mutation exhibited a marked decrease in colony corrugation
source: Strains harboring the D97A and D97K mutations retained the colony corrugation pattern of the rugose parental strain, while strains lacking RbmA (∆rbmA) or harboring the R234A mutation exhibited a marked decrease in colony corrugation (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony biofilm images shown in Figure 3A

claim: ∆rbmA and R234A strains showed uniform spreading in colony corrugation development over time
source: The strains also varied in the colony corrugation development as a function of time, with ∆rbmA and R234A showing uniform spreading, D97A and D97K showing irregular spreading, and the parental rugose strain showing an intermediate spreading phenotype (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, and Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, and Video 1

claim: D97A and D97K strains showed irregular spreading in colony corrugation development over time
source: The strains also varied in the colony corrugation development as a function of time, with ∆rbmA and R234A showing uniform spreading, D97A and D97K showing irregular spreading, and the parental rugose strain showing an intermediate spreading phenotype (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, and Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, and Video 1

claim: The rugose, D97A, and D97K strains all showed similar vertical wave-like features of biomass distribution in dark-field colony images
source: In dark-field colony images of thin sections prepared at 48 hr, the rugose, D97A, and D97K strains all showed similar vertical wave-like features of biomass distribution. In contrast, the internal colony structures of the ∆rbmA and R234A strains were more uniform (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dark-field microscopy images shown in Figure 3B

claim: The internal colony structures of the ∆rbmA and R234A strains were more uniform
source: In dark-field colony images of thin sections prepared at 48 hr, the rugose, D97A, and D97K strains all showed similar vertical wave-like features of biomass distribution. In contrast, the internal colony structures of the ∆rbmA and R234A strains were more uniform (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dark-field microscopy images shown in Figure 3B

claim: Colony heights were similar among all of the strains tested
source: Although colony heights were similar among all of the strains tested (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E), colony outgrowth of D97 mutants was reduced when compared to the parental rugose strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony height measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E

claim: Colony outgrowth of D97 mutants was reduced when compared to the parental rugose strain
source: Although colony heights were similar among all of the strains tested (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E), colony outgrowth of D97 mutants was reduced when compared to the parental rugose strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observation of colony images

claim: Both ∆rbmA and R234A strains formed micro-colonies with edges that are more smooth and regularly-shaped as opposed to the irregularly-shaped micro-colonies observed in the parental strain
source: Both ∆rbmA and R234A strains formed micro-colonies with edges that are more smooth and regularly-shaped as opposed to the irregularly-shaped micro-colonies observed in the parental strain (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 3C

claim: Mature biofilms formed by ∆rbmA and R234A were less structured and exhibited a decrease in biomass and thickness
source: Quantitative and microscopic analysis of mature biofilms formed by ∆rbmA and R234A revealed that they were less structured and exhibited a decrease in biomass and thickness; the biofilm properties of D97A/D97K mutants more closely resembled that of the parental strain (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and microscopy images shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: The biofilm properties of D97A/D97K mutants more closely resembled that of the parental strain
source: Quantitative and microscopic analysis of mature biofilms formed by ∆rbmA and R234A revealed that they were less structured and exhibited a decrease in biomass and thickness; the biofilm properties of D97A/D97K mutants more closely resembled that of the parental strain (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and microscopy images shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Biofilms of R234A and ∆rbmA strains exhibited increased cell detachment, resulting in higher colony forming units (CFU) per effluent volume when compared to the parental strain and D97A/D97K mutants
source: Biofilms of R234A and ∆rbmA strains also exhibited increased cell detachment, resulting in higher colony forming units (CFU) per effluent volume when compared to the parental strain and D97A/D97K mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D

claim: Nearest-neighbor distance is increased in the following order: rugose, D97K, D97A, ∆rbmA, R234A
source: Nearest-neighbor distance, which is a measure of average cell-cell spacing (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Video 2), is increased in the following order: rugose, D97K, D97A, ∆rbmA, R234A.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell resolution microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Video 2

claim: Cells in direct contact with the glass substratum are vertically oriented in the R234A mutant
source: Examination of internal cell arrangements in the biofilm revealed that cells in direct contact with the glass substratum are vertically oriented in the R234A mutant (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell resolution microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Vertical orientation of cells in contact with the substratum is also displayed by the ∆rbmA strain, albeit to a lesser extent
source: Such vertical orientation of cells in contact with the substratum is also displayed by the ∆rbmA strain, albeit to a lesser extent.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell resolution microscopy analysis

claim: Cells of the rugose strain that are in contact with the substratum are mostly radially aligned and horizontal
source: By contrast, cells of the rugose strain that are in contact with the substratum are mostly radially aligned and horizontal.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell resolution microscopy analysis

claim: R234A exhibits a nearly crystal-like cellular alignment in the center and at the bottom of the biofilm
source: With respect to local nematic order, a measure of the degree of local alignment of the cells (see definition in the Materials and Methods), R234A exhibits a nearly crystal-like cellular alignment in the center and at the bottom of the biofilm (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by nematic order analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: Decreased nematic order with the D-loop locked mutants and wild-type RbmA strain suggests that sampling the O-loop conformation leads to decreases in local cell alignment
source: By contrast, decreased nematic order with the D-loop locked mutants and wild-type RbmA strain suggests that sampling the O-loop conformation leads to decreases in local cell alignment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from nematic order analysis data

claim: For rugose, D97A, and D97K strains, the RbmA localization was similar, where RbmA is distributed between the surface of the biofilm and the center of the biofilm
source: For rugose, D97A, and D97K strains, the RbmA localization was similar, where RbmA is distributed between the surface of the biofilm and the center of the biofilm (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 4C

claim: In the R234A strain, RbmA abundance was high at the center of the biofilm, and decreased towards the surface
source: In contrast, in the R234A strain, RbmA abundance was high at the center of the biofilm, and decreased towards the surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Changes in the conformation and/or dimerization state of RbmA alter biofilm architectural properties
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that changes in the conformation and/or dimerization state of RbmA alter biofilm architectural properties.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple biofilm characterization experiments

claim: Locking RbmA in the closed, O-loop dimer state with the R234A mutation severely affects biofilm formation
source: Locking RbmA in the closed, O-loop dimer state with the R234A mutation severely affects biofilm formation, while the locked, monomer D-loop state (D97A/D97K) more closely resembles the native role of RbmA in biofilm regulation and that differences in biofilm architecture could be due to changes in RbmA localization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from biofilm characterization data

claim: The locked, monomer D-loop state (D97A/D97K) more closely resembles the native role of RbmA in biofilm regulation
source: Locking RbmA in the closed, O-loop dimer state with the R234A mutation severely affects biofilm formation, while the locked, monomer D-loop state (D97A/D97K) more closely resembles the native role of RbmA in biofilm regulation and that differences in biofilm architecture could be due to changes in RbmA localization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from biofilm characterization data

claim: Addition of VPS induced uniform peak broadening in 15N RbmA spectra, consistent with formation of higher-order soluble oligomers
source: We found that addition of VPS induced uniform peak broadening in 15N RbmA spectra, consistent with formation of higher-order soluble oligomers (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Similar changes in peak intensity were also observed in VPS binding experiments with 15N RbmA R234A
source: Similar changes in peak intensity were also observed in VPS binding experiments with 15N RbmA R234A, suggesting that remarkable functional differences between WT and R234A RbmA might not lie in its ability to bind VPS.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The extent of peak broadening correlates with formation of the locked species
source: Integrating peak intensity from either the amide region (11 to 5.5 p.p.m.) (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) or side chain region (2.5 to −1 p.p.m.) (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) of the 1H spectra demonstrated that the extent of peak broadening correlates with formation of the locked species.
evidence: The claim is supported by 1D 1H NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5B, 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Binding to VPS by RbmA results in the formation of higher-order RbmA-VPS structures that are governed by the structural dynamics of the binary switch in RbmA
source: Based on these data, we suggest that binding to VPS by RbmA results in the formation of higher-order RbmA-VPS structures that are governed by the structural dynamics of the binary switch in RbmA.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from NMR spectroscopy data showing VPS-dependent oligomerization

claim: VPS is localized around cell clusters in the rugose, D97A and D97K strains
source: We found that VPS is localized around cell clusters in the rugose, D97A and D97K strains (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5D

claim: In the R234A strain, VPS localization was diffuse and reduced
source: However, in the R234A strain, VPS localization was diffuse and reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Structural properties of RbmA affects VPS localization in biofilms
source: These findings suggest that structural properties of RbmA affects VPS localization in biofilms.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from VPS localization data

claim: The full-length protein can undergo spontaneous cleavage in the FnIII-1 domain near the interdomain linker
source: We observed that the full-length protein can undergo spontaneous cleavage in the FnIII-1 domain near the interdomain linker (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C), resulting in a highly stable 13 kDa protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR and gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: The 15N-1H HSQC spectrum of the cleaved form closely resembles the RbmA* variant
source: Importantly, the 15N-1H HSQC spectrum of the cleaved form closely resembles the RbmA* variant, although it lacked the poorly dispersed peaks in the center of the spectrum (8.0–8.5 p.p.m.) that correspond to the unfolded FnIII-1 fragment remaining in RbmA* (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–I

claim: Well-resolved peaks in the RbmA* spectrum exhibited marked similarity to the isolated 15N FnIII-2 domain
source: Well-resolved peaks in the RbmA* spectrum also exhibited marked similarity to the isolated 15N FnIII-2 domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data

claim: An 15N-1H HSQC spectrum of the isolated 15N FnIII-1 domain exhibited poor chemical shift dispersion and a tendency to form soluble aggregates, indicating that this domain is not stably folded in isolation
source: An 15N-1H HSQC spectrum of the isolated 15N FnIII-1 domain exhibited poor chemical shift dispersion and a tendency to form soluble aggregates, indicating that this domain is not stably folded in isolation.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data and inference about protein folding

claim: The FnIII-2 domain is the stable core domain of RbmA and its natively processed form, RbmA*
source: Altogether, these data suggest that the FnIII-2 domain is the stable core domain of RbmA and its natively processed form, RbmA*, possibly regulates the structural integrity of the FnIII-1 domain through formation of the dimer.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from NMR spectroscopy data

claim: RbmA* possibly regulates the structural integrity of the FnIII-1 domain through formation of the dimer
source: Altogether, these data suggest that the FnIII-2 domain is the stable core domain of RbmA and its natively processed form, RbmA*, possibly regulates the structural integrity of the FnIII-1 domain through formation of the dimer.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from structural data

claim: Addition of VPS induced dose-dependent chemical shift perturbations in 15N RbmA* consistent with VPS binding
source: We collected 15N-1H HSQC spectra of 15N RbmA* in the presence and absence of VPS, observing a number of dose-dependent chemical shift perturbations consistent with VPS binding; the same chemical shifts were also found upon titration of VPS into the isolated 15N FnIII-2 domain (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The same chemical shifts were also found upon titration of VPS into the isolated 15N FnIII-2 domain
source: We collected 15N-1H HSQC spectra of 15N RbmA* in the presence and absence of VPS, observing a number of dose-dependent chemical shift perturbations consistent with VPS binding; the same chemical shifts were also found upon titration of VPS into the isolated 15N FnIII-2 domain (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Residues with significant VPS-dependent chemical shift perturbations form one contiguous patch on the exposed outer surface of the FnIII-2 domain that likely constitutes the VPS binding site
source: When mapped onto the crystal structure of the RbmA dimer, these residues form one contiguous patch on the exposed outer surface of the FnIII-2 domain that likely constitutes the VPS binding site (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from NMR chemical shift perturbation data mapped onto the crystal structure shown in Figure 6D

claim: The VPS binding interface is distinct from that used to form the RbmA dimer through interaction with the FnIII-1 domain
source: This interface is distinct from that used to form the RbmA dimer through interaction with the FnIII-1 domain.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural analysis

claim: The presence of two VPS-binding motifs on each RbmA dimer suggests the possibility for multivalent binding to VPS
source: The presence of two such motifs on each RbmA dimer therefore suggests the possibility for multivalent binding to VPS.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from structural analysis

claim: Solution studies of RbmA have demonstrated that the two halves of the dimer, separated by flexible interdomain linkers, can open to form an extended conformation
source: Moreover, solution studies of RbmA have demonstrated that the two halves of the dimer, separated by flexible interdomain linkers, can open to form an extended conformation (Figure 6E), suggesting that the VPS-binding interface could regulate RbmA function by possibly contributing to the formation of different conformations in solution.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous solution studies and shown in Figure 6E

claim: The VPS-binding interface could regulate RbmA function by possibly contributing to the formation of different conformations in solution
source: Moreover, solution studies of RbmA have demonstrated that the two halves of the dimer, separated by flexible interdomain linkers, can open to form an extended conformation (Figure 6E), suggesting that the VPS-binding interface could regulate RbmA function by possibly contributing to the formation of different conformations in solution.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from structural data
